newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ firming signal sent due to rapid change - Birch.
newsitem.headline: NZ firming signal sent due to rapid change - Birch.

text.p: New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch told Reuters Financial Television in Fukuoka on Tuesday that a recent rapid easing in debt and currency market-driven monetary conditions had led to the Reserve Bank sending a firming signal on Monday.

Birch, in Japan for the Asian Development Bank annual meeting, was commenting on a statement by the Reserve Bank which said monetary conditions had settled too far from desired levels and it wanted them somewhat firmer.

Birch said market interest rates had fallen very quickly, with 90-day bill rates dipping "well under" 7.0 percent recently, while the currency's Trade-Weighted Index, which had been very stable, had also come back slightly.
"The combination of both those factors led the Reserve Bank to say monetary conditions are loosening more than they would like," he said.
He also judged the upcoming June budget as unlikely to put any undue pressure on monetary policy.
And, looking to the Reserve Bank's scheduled June Monetary Policy Statement (MPS), Birch said he was working on the basis of it containing "no great surprise" for monetary conditions.
While he declined to specify the date of the budget in June when asked, he said he still expected it would show significant surpluses despite planned spending increases.
"We are not going to put undue pressure on the monetary policy conditions," he said.
He said the budget would certainly not affect New Zealand's prospects of achieving a triple A credit rating in time.
Commenting on Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash's MPS, due in June close to the budget, Birch said he himself was working on the expectation of little change.

"(Brash) will be looking very closely at the economic indicators. He has given a very strong signal of the level that he's comfortable with in terms of monetary policy settings, and he'll be moving forward to achieve those.
"I'll be working on the basis of no great surprises (in the statement)," Birch said.
